arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: General Mukasey argued the lower court added an element. He said the statute does not require a direct link. He claimed the word during is purely temporal.
Mr. Hillier argued the lower court acted correctly. He said the lie must relate to the crime. He claimed the government tried to charge a sure thing.
Justice Breyer asked if a foreseeable relationship is enough. He suggested the explosives made the lie necessary. He tested the boundary of the legal requirement.
Justice Ginsburg asked why prosecutors chose this specific charge. She questioned the logical link to the false statement. She explored the prosecutor's strategic decision.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the meaning of a federal law. The law adds prison time for lying about explosives. The dispute centers on the word during. The government says this word marks time. The defendant says it marks a relationship. The lower court sided with the defendant. The government seeks to remove that requirement.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The government wants the lower court to drop the extra requirement. It wants the conviction to stand as originally found.
The defendant wants the lower court to keep the extra requirement. It wants the conviction to fail because of that gap.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The government argues the statute only needs a time connection. It claims the lower court added words not in the law.
The defendant argues the statute needs a direct relationship. It claims the lie must relate to the specific crime.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case defines how courts read federal sentencing laws. It clarifies when a false statement triggers extra prison time. It sets a standard for linking lies to specific criminal acts. It affects how prosecutors build cases involving explosives. It shapes the balance between statutory text and judicial interpretation.
